newsitem.title: POLAND: Forecasts offer hope amid rain over flooded Poland.
newsitem.headline: Forecasts offer hope amid rain over flooded Poland.

text.p: Heavy rain continued on Saturday over large tracts of Poland already devastated by flooding, but weather reports offered hopes of avoiding a return to the nightmare of the past two weeks.

"Reports...show there is no danger of such a wave (of floods), of such water as we remember a week ago," President Aleksander Kwasniewski told reporters after a briefing from Poland's flood crisis committee in Warsaw.
The rains on Friday and into the weekend sent communities of Poland's ravaged south and west back on to disaster alert and some reported they were starting to be flooded anew.
Several villages in Zielona Gora province were told to evacuate after a dyke broke. Some streets of the lower Silesia mining town of Walbrzych were again under water.

Bitter experience meant that this time the government and hundreds of thousands of Poles in affected areas were taking few chances. Troops were helping citizens build sandbag barriers and strengthen weakened dykes.

In Opole on the river Odra, where two metres of water raged around high-rise city-centre buildings last week, authorities told citizens to listen for three-minute siren warnings -- after which they would have an hour to reach evacuation points.
But crisis committee officials said latest forecasts suggested the rains were less heavy than first feared and would shift to the less vulnerable centre of Poland or end by Sunday.
Deputy Environment Minister Krzysztof Szamalek, a committee chief, said any renewed flooding would be on a scale that could be dealt with, PAP news agency reported.
The first wave of floods this month was an unexpected deluge that killed 49 people, swamped 4,000 sq km and hit a thousand villages and towns, including major cities.
The have jolted the zloty currency, caused the government to arrange extra borrowing and raised questions over whether parliamentary polls should be held as planned on September 21.
Kwasniewski said that unless something very unexpected happened he would not declare a state of emergency in affected areas, which would automatically delay the elections.

Many towns and villages hit by floods are too preoccupied with their own drama to worry about politics and some people are embittered against the government led by ex-communists over the extent of support they got at the outset.
But Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, said that in two months affected communities would be able to hold elections.
"I don't want to talk about the mood or the way people will vote, but organisationally it is possible," he said. Delayed polls would give a bad signal about Poland's democracy.
The elections will pit the ruling ex-communists against a strong alliance built around the Solidarity trade union, which is strongly critical of the government's crisis-management.
